subject: Climate & Environment
title: Phytoplankton: The Invisible Powerhouse
description: A short lesson to help you apply Phytoplankton: The Invisible Powerhouse.

hook.text: Phytoplankton are microscopic. Yet they produce more oxygen than all the forests on Earth combined.

buildup.text: These tiny algae float near the surface, using sunlight and CO₂ to grow through photosynthesis.

discovery.text: When they die, some sink to the deep ocean, locking carbon away for centuries — the biological pump.

twist.text: Phytoplankton populations have declined 40% since 1950 as ocean temperatures have risen.

climax.text: Losing phytoplankton means less oxygen, less carbon storage, and a collapsing marine food chain.

punchline.text: The creatures you can't see are the ones keeping you alive.

quiz.question: How much have phytoplankton populations declined since 1950?

details.summary: Phytoplankton are microscopic marine plants that produce roughly half of the world's oxygen through photosynthesis. They form the base of the ocean food web and draw CO2 from the atmosphere, exporting carbon to the deep sea when they die and sink.
details.whyItMatters: Despite their tiny size, phytoplankton underpin global oxygen supply and marine fisheries. Declines in phytoplankton threaten both climate stability and food security.
takeaways: Phytoplankton generate about half of Earth's oxygen
They are the foundation of nearly every marine food chain
Sinking dead cells export carbon to the deep ocean

faq.question: Are phytoplankton populations declining?
faq.answer: Some studies report a roughly one-percent annual decline in global phytoplankton over the past century, linked to warming and increased stratification that reduces nutrient supply to the surface. Trends vary by region.

faq.question: How do phytoplankton remove CO2 from the atmosphere?
faq.answer: Phytoplankton absorb dissolved CO2 during photosynthesis. When they die, their carbon-rich remains sink to the deep ocean floor, effectively locking carbon away from the atmosphere for centuries in a process called the biological pump.
